s0003.literal: Hu Ying; Xu Du; son Jingcheng; Du Leng; Shen Ke
s0003.idiomatic: Hu Ying; Xu Du; son Jingcheng; Du Leng; Shen Ke

s0004.literal: Hu Ying, styled Fangxiu, was a native of Dongqian in Wuxing.
s0004.idiomatic: Hu Ying, styled Fangxiu, came from Dongqian in Wuxing.

s0005.literal: His forebears had sojourned in Wuxing; when the native register was discontinued they were accounted local people.
s0005.idiomatic: His family had long lived in Wuxing as sojourners; after the register was broken off they were reckoned natives of the place.

s0006.literal: Ying had a grand bearing and handsome looks, and a generous disposition.
s0006.idiomatic: Ying was tall and striking, with an open, generous nature.

s0007.literal: Under Liang he rose to Vice-Minister in the state of Wuling and Direct Attendant Before the Eastern Palace.
s0007.idiomatic: Under Liang he served as vice-minister in the state of Wuling and direct attendant before the Eastern Palace.

s0008.literal: He went out from Panyu to campaign against the Li cave settlements. As West River defense commander of Guangzhou, when the Founder was at Guangzhou Ying attached himself to him of his own accord; the Founder was from the same commandery and received him with great favor.
s0008.idiomatic: Posted from Panyu against the Li caves, he held the West River defense command at Guangzhou. When the Founder was there, Ying sought him out on his own. They shared a home commandery, and the Founder treated him with exceptional warmth.

s0009.literal: When the southern campaign against Jiaozhi was launched, Ying followed on campaign; the other generals all ranked below him.
s0009.idiomatic: On the march to Jiaozhi he went with the army, and the other commanders stood beneath him in rank.

s0010.literal: When Li Ben was pacified the Founder withdrew his army; Ying remained subordinate on the West River, and whenever troops marched out Ying was often left to hold the rear.
s0010.idiomatic: After Li Ben fell the Founder turned homeward. Ying stayed on the West River, and in most campaigns he was left behind to guard the base.

s0011.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion the Founder captured Yuan Jingzhong, then crossed the ranges to relieve the Terrace City, and pacified Cai Luyang and Li Qianshi; Ying had merit in all of this.
s0011.idiomatic: During Hou Jing's rebellion the Founder took Yuan Jingzhong, crossed the mountains to relieve the capital, and crushed Cai Luyang and Li Qianshi. Ying earned merit in every fight.

s0012.literal: He served successively as magistrate of the two counties of Pinggu and Suixing.
s0012.idiomatic: He served in turn as magistrate of Pinggu and Suixing.

s0013.literal: When the Founder advanced his army and halted at Xichang, he made Ying magistrate of Baqiu, garrisoned Dago, and supervised grain transport.
s0013.idiomatic: When the Founder marched and camped at Xichang, he made Ying magistrate of Baqiu, posted him at Dago, and put him in charge of grain convoys.

s0014.literal: Descending to Yuzhang, he made Ying overseer of Yuzhang commandery.
s0014.idiomatic: Moving downriver to Yuzhang, he appointed Ying overseer of the commandery.

s0015.literal: The Founder led his host to meet Wang Sengbian at Baimao Bay to campaign jointly against Hou Jing, and put Ying in charge of affairs left at headquarters.
s0015.idiomatic: The Founder took his army to Baimao Bay to join Wang Sengbian against Hou Jing and left Ying to manage headquarters.

s0016.literal: Ying's younger brother Shuo also followed Ying as a general.
s0016.idiomatic: Ying's younger brother Shuo followed him into the ranks as a general.

s0017.literal: When Ying died, Shuo took command of his troops.
s0017.idiomatic: When Ying died, Shuo inherited his command.

s0018.literal: He served successively as administrator of the two commanderies of Donghai and Yuzhang, and was promoted to supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant.
s0018.idiomatic: He governed Donghai and Yuzhang in turn, then rose to supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0019.literal: He followed Zhang Zhaoda in the southern pacification of Ouyang He, Editorial footnote marker 3. and was made East River defense commander of Guangzhou.
s0019.idiomatic: He marched south with Zhang Zhaoda to crush Ouyang He [3] and was made East River defense commander of Guangzhou.

s0020.literal: Returning, he took part in the northern campaign and was made Trustworthy-Faith General and Administrator of Liyang.
s0020.idiomatic: Back from the south he joined the northern campaign and was appointed trustworthy-faith general and administrator of Liyang.

s0021.literal: In the sixth year of Taijian he died; posthumously he was given Inspector of Gui.
s0021.idiomatic: He died in Taijian year 6 (574) and was posthumously made inspector of Gui.

s0022.literal: Xu Du, styled Xiaojie, was a native of Anlu.
s0022.idiomatic: Xu Du, styled Xiaojie, came from Anlu.

s0023.literal: For generations his family dwelt in the capital.
s0023.idiomatic: His family had lived in the capital for generations.

s0024.literal: In youth he was bold and free, heedless of small proprieties.
s0024.idiomatic: As a youth he was reckless and bold, careless of petty rules.

s0025.literal: When grown, his looks were magnificent; he loved wine and gambling and constantly set his servants to butchering and brewing for his pleasure.
s0025.idiomatic: Grown to manhood he was imposing in bearing, fond of wine and dice, and kept servants busy slaughtering and brewing for his table.

s0026.literal: When Xiao Jie of Liang was interior minister of Shixing and went to his commandery, Du followed him, leading troops in campaigns against the mountain caves, and won a name for fierce courage.
s0026.idiomatic: When Liang's interior minister of Shixing, Xiao Jie, took up his post, Du went with him, commanding men against the hill tribes, and became known for daring.

s0027.literal: When the Founder campaigned against Jiaozhi he treated Du with generous courtesy to win him; Du then offered his allegiance.
s0027.idiomatic: On the Jiaozhi campaign the Founder courted him with rich gifts; Du at last pledged himself.

s0028.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion the Founder secured Guangzhou, pacified Cai Luyang, and broke Li Qianshi; much of the planning came from Du.
s0028.idiomatic: In Hou Jing's rising the Founder held Guangzhou, crushed Cai Luyang, and routed Li Qianshi. Du supplied much of the strategy.

s0029.literal: He also took overall command of armor and weapons; in every battle he had merit.
s0029.idiomatic: He also commanded the armorers and fought with merit in every engagement.

s0030.literal: Returning to Baimao Bay, Emperor Yuan of Liang appointed him Pacifying-the-North General and Inspector of He.
s0030.idiomatic: Back at Baimao Bay, Emperor Yuan of Liang made him pacifying-the-north general and inspector of He.

s0031.literal: After Hou Jing was pacified, his earlier and later battle achievements were entered in the record; he was promoted to direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant, enfeoffed as Marquis of Guangde county with a fief of five hundred households.
s0031.idiomatic: Once Hou Jing fell, past and recent victories were tallied. He was raised to direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant and enfeoffed as Marquis of Guangde with five hundred households.

s0032.literal: He was transferred to scattered-cavalry regular attendant.
s0032.idiomatic: He was transferred to scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0033.literal: Xu Siwei, Ren Yue, and others came to raid; the Founder and Emperor Jing returned to the capital.
s0033.idiomatic: Xu Siwei, Ren Yue, and others struck at the capital. The Founder and Emperor Jing came back to defend it.

s0034.literal: At that time the rebels already held Shitou citadel; market towns and residents along the southern road lay far from the Terrace City, and there was fear they would be seized by the rebels; Du was therefore sent with troops to garrison Yecheng Temple and build a stockade to cut them off.
s0034.idiomatic: The rebels already held Shitou. Markets and towns on the southern road lay far from the palace, open to being overrun, so Du was sent with troops to Yecheng Temple to build a wall and block the approach.

s0035.literal: The rebels mustered their full strength to attack but could not overcome him.
s0035.idiomatic: The rebels threw their whole force against him and failed to break through.

s0036.literal: The Founder soon came to the rescue as well and inflicted a great defeat on Ren Yue and the others.
s0036.idiomatic: The Founder soon arrived in relief and routed Ren Yue and his allies.

s0037.literal: The next year Siwei and the others again brought Northern Qi raiders across the river; Du followed the mass of armies and defeated them at the North Suburbs altar.
s0037.idiomatic: The next year Siwei again drew Qi troops across the Yangzi. Du marched with the main host and beat them at the North Suburbs altar.

s0038.literal: For merit he was made Trustworthy-Power General and Inspector of Ying, and concurrently Administrator of Wuxing.
s0038.idiomatic: For merit he was made trustworthy-power general and inspector of Ying, and also administrator of Wuxing.

s0039.literal: Soon he was transferred to Suppressing-the-Right General, Commandant of the Guards, Commander of Military Affairs along the Yangzi bank of Xuzhou, Editorial footnote marker 4. Suppressing-the-North General, and Inspector of South Xuzhou, and was given one set of martial pipes and drums.
s0039.idiomatic: He was soon made suppressing-the-right general, commandant of the guards, commander along the Yangzi frontier of Xuzhou, [4] suppressing-the-north general, and inspector of South Xuzhou, with a full set of pipes and drums.

s0040.literal: When Emperor Wen died, Du was named in the final testament; fifty men with arms and armor entered the palace offices.
s0040.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen died, Du was named in the deathbed testament. Fifty armed guards were posted in the palace offices.

s0041.literal: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne, Du was advanced to Minister of Works.
s0041.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor succeeded, Du was promoted to minister of works.

s0042.literal: Hua Jiao held Xiangzhou in rebellion and brought Zhou troops down to Chun Ford, where they faced the royal army in stalemate; Du was then given credentials, made Chariots-and-Cavalry General, and put in overall command of the infantry. From Ancheng commandery he took the ridge route out into eastern Xiang to strike Xiangzhou and brought back all the army households and dependents Jiao had left behind.
s0042.idiomatic: Hua Jiao rebelled in Xiangzhou and drew Zhou armies to Chun Ford, where they locked with the imperial host. Du was given credentials as chariots-and-cavalry general and made commander of all foot troops. He marched from Ancheng over the ridges into eastern Xiang, raided Xiangzhou, and carried off every soldier's family Jiao had left there.

s0043.literal: In the second year of Guangda he died, aged sixty.
s0043.idiomatic: He died in Guangda year 2 (567), aged sixty.

s0044.literal: Posthumously he was given Grand Commandant, twenty ritual swords, and the posthumous title Loyal and Solemn.
s0044.idiomatic: He was posthumously made grand commandant, granted twenty ritual swords, and given the posthumous name Loyal and Solemn.

s0045.literal: In the fourth year of Taijian he was given a place in the Founder's temple hall.
s0045.idiomatic: In Taijian year 4 (572) he was enshrined in the Founder's temple.

s0046.idiomatic: His son Jingcheng inherited the line.

s0047.literal: In the fifth year he was made Upright-Power General and Administrator of Wuxing.
s0047.idiomatic: In the fifth year he was made upright-power general and administrator of Wuxing.

s0048.literal: That year he followed the commander-in-chief Wu Mingche on the northern campaign, marching out of Qin commandery; Jingcheng was separately dispatched as commander, taking the Golden Wings from Ouyangyin Dam upriver by way of Guangling.
s0048.idiomatic: That year he marched north under Wu Mingche, leaving from Qin commandery. Jingcheng was sent as a separate commander, sailing the Golden Wings from Ouyangyin Dam up the Yangzi through Guangling.

s0049.literal: The Qi men all held their cities and dared not come out.
s0049.idiomatic: The Qi forces shut themselves in their walled towns and would not fight.

s0050.literal: From Fanliang Lake he descended the Huai and besieged Huaiyin city.
s0050.idiomatic: From Fanliang Lake he went down the Huai and laid siege to Huaiyin.

s0051.literal: He was then made overseer of North Yanzhou.
s0051.idiomatic: He was then made overseer of North Yanzhou.

s0052.literal: Righteous militia of Huai and Si rose in answer one after another; within a day or two their numbers reached tens of thousands; he then took the three commanderies of Huaiyin, Shanyang, and Yancheng, and the two garrisons of Lian Ford and Qushan.
s0052.idiomatic: Loyal levies on the Huai and Si rallied to him by the thousand. In a day or two he had tens of thousands of men and seized Huaiyin, Shanyang, and Yancheng, with the garrisons at Lian Ford and Qushan.

s0053.literal: He then advanced to attack Yuzhou and took it.
s0053.idiomatic: He pressed on to Yuzhou and captured it.

s0054.literal: For merit he was promoted to direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant and Cloud-Banner General, and his fief was increased by five hundred households.
s0054.idiomatic: For merit he was made direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant and cloud-banner general, with five hundred more households in his fief.

s0055.literal: His title was further advanced to Stalwart-Martial General, and he garrisoned Qushan.
s0055.idiomatic: He was further promoted to stalwart-martial general and posted at Qushan.

s0056.literal: Because in camp he arbitrarily imposed punishments and also executed newly submitted men, he was removed from office.
s0056.idiomatic: He was dismissed for summarily punishing men in camp and executing fresh recruits.

s0057.literal: Soon he was again made with credentials, Area Commander over Military Affairs in the three provinces of An, Yuan, and Tong, Inspector of An, general as before, garrisoning Suyu.
s0057.idiomatic: Soon he was restored with credentials as area commander of An, Yuan, and Tong, inspector of An, with his old rank, garrisoning Suyu.

s0058.literal: In the seventh year he died, aged thirty-six.
s0058.idiomatic: He died in the seventh year, aged thirty-six.

s0059.literal: Posthumously he was given scattered-cavalry regular attendant, with the posthumous title Reflective.
s0059.idiomatic: He was posthumously made scattered-cavalry regular attendant and given the posthumous name Reflective.

s0061.literal: Du Leng, styled Xiongsheng, was a native of Qiantang in Wu commandery.
s0061.idiomatic: Du Leng, styled Xiongsheng, came from Qiantang in Wu commandery.

s0062.literal: For generations his clan was a great surname of the county.
s0062.idiomatic: For generations his clan was one of the county's great families.

s0063.literal: Leng had dipped into books and records; in youth he was adrift and unknown to his age.
s0063.idiomatic: Leng had read widely, but in youth he drifted without notice.

s0064.literal: He then traveled to Lingnan and served Liang's Inspector of Guangzhou, the Prince of Xinyu, Xiao Ying.
s0064.idiomatic: He went south to Lingnan and entered the service of Liang's inspector of Guangzhou, the Prince of Xinyu, Xiao Ying.

s0065.literal: When Ying died he followed the Founder and constantly kept the written records.
s0065.idiomatic: When Ying died he followed the Founder and served constantly as his secretary.

s0066.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion he was ordered to take command; pacifying Cai Luyang and Li Qianshi, he had merit in both.
s0066.idiomatic: In Hou Jing's rebellion he was put in command. He helped crush Cai Luyang and Li Qianshi and won merit in both campaigns.

s0067.literal: When the army reached Yuzhang, Emperor Yuan of Liang, acting on the regency commission, appointed Leng Benevolent-Power General and Inspector of Shi, enfeoffed him as Marquis of Shangmo county with a fief of eight hundred households.
s0067.idiomatic: At Yuzhang, Emperor Yuan of Liang, exercising regency powers, made Leng benevolent-power general and inspector of Shi, and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Shangmo with eight hundred households.

s0068.literal: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne, he was transferred to Suppressing-the-Right General and Special Grandee, palace attendant and metropolitan governor unchanged.
s0068.idiomatic: When the Deposed Emperor succeeded, he was made suppressing-the-right general and special grandee, retaining his posts as palace attendant and metropolitan governor.

s0069.literal: In the first year of Guangda he was relieved of the governorship; a full staff of aides was appointed, supports were granted, and he was again given Commandant of the Guards.
s0069.idiomatic: In Guangda year 1 (567) he left the metropolitan post. A full staff was assigned, carriage supports granted, and he was again made commandant of the guards.

s0070.literal: In the first year of Taijian he went out as scattered-cavalry regular attendant, Suppressing-the-East General, and Administrator of Wuxing, with salary of middle two thousand dan.
s0070.idiomatic: In Taijian year 1 (569) he was sent out as scattered-cavalry regular attendant, suppressing-the-east general, and administrator of Wuxing, at middle two-thousand-dan rank.

s0071.literal: In the second year he was summoned to be palace attendant and Suppressing-the-Right General.
s0071.idiomatic: In the second year he was recalled as palace attendant and suppressing-the-right general.

s0072.literal: Soon he was further given special grandee and Protector of the Army.
s0072.idiomatic: Soon he was also made special grandee and protector of the army.

s0073.literal: In the third year, on public business he was removed from palace attendant and protector of the army.
s0073.idiomatic: In the third year he was dismissed from palace attendant and protector of the army on official grounds.

s0074.literal: In the fourth year he was again made palace attendant and Right Grandee for Splendid Virtue, and was also given one set of martial pipes and drums; general, staff, and supports were all as before.
s0074.idiomatic: In the fourth year he returned as palace attendant and right grandee for splendid virtue, with pipes and drums restored; his rank, staff, and carriage supports stayed as before.

s0075.literal: Leng served three emperors and in each was shown favor.
s0075.idiomatic: Leng served three emperors and won favor under each.

s0076.literal: In his last years he took no part in campaigns; he lived at ease in the capital, and gifts and rewards were generous.
s0076.idiomatic: In his last years he stayed out of the field, idling in the capital while honors and gifts flowed freely.

s0077.literal: Before long he died in office, aged seventy.
s0077.idiomatic: He soon died in office, aged seventy.

s0078.literal: Posthumously he was given Grand Master for Splendid Happiness with the same ceremonial as the Three Excellencies; all funeral needs were ordered supplied, and his posthumous title was Accomplished.
s0078.idiomatic: He was posthumously made grand master for splendid happiness with three-excellency honors; the court paid for the funeral and gave him the posthumous name Accomplished.

s0079.literal: That year he was given a place in the Founder's temple hall.
s0079.idiomatic: That year he was enshrined in the Founder's temple.

s0081.literal: Shen Ke, styled Zigong, was a native of Wukang in Wuxing.
s0081.idiomatic: Shen Ke, styled Zigong, came from Wukang in Wuxing.

s0082.literal: He was deep and steady, with administrative capacity.
s0082.idiomatic: He was reserved and steady, with a gift for command.

s0083.literal: When Liang's Prince of Xinyu, Xiao Ying, was commandery general, Ke was summoned as chief clerk.
s0083.idiomatic: When Liang's Prince of Xinyu, Xiao Ying, held a commandery, Ke was called up as chief clerk.

s0084.literal: When Ying was transferred to North Xuzhou, Ke followed Ying to his garrison.
s0084.idiomatic: When Ying moved to North Xuzhou, Ke went with him to the post.

s0085.literal: When Ying was transferred to Guangzhou, Ke was made concurrent military adjutant in the establishment and constantly led troops to campaign against the Li cave settlements.
s0085.idiomatic: When Ying went to Guangzhou, Ke was made concurrent military adjutant in the princely staff and often led troops against the Li caves.

s0086.literal: When Lu Zilüe rebelled, Ke resisted in battle and had merit; he was made middle military adjutant.
s0086.idiomatic: When Lu Zilüe rose, Ke fought him off with merit and was made middle military adjutant.

s0087.literal: The Founder was from the same commandery and was on very close terms with Ke; after Xiao Ying died the Founder campaigned south against Li Ben and sent his wife and children home with Ke to their native place.
s0087.idiomatic: The Founder shared Ke's home commandery and liked him well. After Xiao Ying died, on the march against Li Ben he sent his family home under Ke's escort.

s0088.literal: Soon he was appointed Direct Attendant After the Eastern Palace; for his merit in Lingnan he was made supernumerary scattered-cavalry attendant gentleman and was further ordered to gather kinsmen and clan youths.
s0088.idiomatic: He was soon made direct attendant after the Eastern Palace, then brevetted scattered-cavalry attendant gentleman for his southern service and told to rally his clan.

s0090.literal: When Hou Jing besieged the Terrace City, Ke led his command into the city and, by precedent, was promoted to Right Army General.
s0090.idiomatic: When Hou Jing besieged the capital, Ke brought his men inside the walls and, by precedent, was made right army general.

s0091.literal: The rebels raised eastern and western earthen hills to press the walls; within the city earthen hills were also built in answer; Ke was master of the eastern hill and fought off attacks day and night.
s0091.idiomatic: The rebels piled earthen mounts east and west against the walls; the defenders raised mounts of their own. Ke held the eastern mound and fought day and night.

s0092.literal: For merit he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dongxing county with a fief of five hundred households.
s0092.idiomatic: For merit he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dongxing with five hundred households.

s0093.literal: He was transferred to supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant.
s0093.idiomatic: He was made supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0094.literal: When the capital fell, Ke slipped away by hidden paths and returned to his home district.
s0094.idiomatic: When the capital fell, Ke stole home by back roads.

s0095.literal: When the Founder campaigned against Hou Jing he sent envoys to notify Ke; Ke then raised troops in the east in response.
s0095.idiomatic: The Founder sent word when he marched against Hou Jing; Ke raised men in the east to join him.

s0096.literal: When the rebels were pacified, Ke called on the Founder at Jingkou and that same day was appointed deputy commander of the capital army.
s0096.idiomatic: After the rebels fell, Ke met the Founder at Jingkou and was named deputy commander of the capital army that same day.
